text.p: British fund management group Mercury Asset Management Tuesday posted a 29 percent jump in first-half pretax profits to 81.8 million pounds ($133.94 million), up from 63.6 million ($104.14) in the first half last year.

It also said its cash rose sharply, to 261.6 million pounds ($428.36 million) from 189.9 million ($310.95 million) at the end of March, raising speculation that the firm might use the surplus to fund expansion in the lucrative U.S. fund management industry, where it already operates.
MAM Chairman Hugh Stevenson said the company would consider acquisitions but only if they increased value for shareholders.
"The U.S. is obviously an extremely important market, it's the biggest savings market in the world, but value for our shareholders is the main aim."
Regarding the increased cash, Stevenson said the company prefers a conservative balance sheet.

"Cash has risen materially in the last six months," he said. "It's a question of a balance between a prudent balance sheet and returning value in the form of dividends to shareholders. We've had a very progressive dividend policy over recent years."
Mercury, which was controlled by investment bank S.G. Warburg before Warburg was bought by Swiss Bank Corp. last year, raised its interim dividend to 10 pence per share from six pence.
About two-thirds of MAM's business is in the institutional pension fund management area, 20 percent for investors overseas and the rest for private investors.

Funds under management rose to 85.9 billion pounds ($140.66 billion) at the end of September compared with 70.9 billion ($116.10 billion) for the same period last year. The most recent figure includes two billion pounds ($3.27 billion) of net new business, which follows its recent growth trend, analysts said.
